title: Recursion and the first steps of dynamic programming
overview: The module starts with recursion: a function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version. Plain recursive Fibonacci repeats the same work many times. Memoization (top-down DP) and a bottom-up loop remove that repeated work. The practice problems apply the same ideas to digits, factorials, reachability and Tribonacci.

concepts.explain: Every recursive function needs a stopping condition (base case) and a call that moves toward it. Without the base case it never stops and the stack overflows.
concepts.snippet: int fact(int n) { if (n == 1) return 1; return n * fact(n - 1); }

concepts.term: Work before vs after the call
concepts.explain: Printing before the recursive call prints in the order the calls are made (1..5). Printing after the call prints as the calls return (5..1).
`fib(n)` calls `fib(n-1)` and `fib(n-2)`, and both of them call `fib(n-3)` again. The plain version takes about 2^n steps.
Keep a `dp` array filled with -1. Before computing, check whether the answer is already stored; after computing, store it. Each state is computed once.
concepts.snippet:
if (dp[n] != -1) return dp[n];
dp[n] = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2);

concepts.explain: Fill the table from the smallest cases upward with a loop. No recursion and no stack depth issues.
Factorials and Fibonacci numbers grow fast. 13! already overflows `int`; use `long long` (good up to 20!).
Drawing the call tree helps you see repeated calls. The module links an online recursion visualiser for this.

files.title: Recursion warm-up: print and sum
files.what: Three small recursive functions: print 1 to 5, print numbers on the way back, and sum 1 to 5.
steps: `print_one_to_five(n)`: stop when `n > 5`; otherwise print `n` and call with `n + 1`.
`print_five_to_one(n)`: call with `n + 1` first, print afterwards, so output appears while returning.
files.complexity: Time O(k) · Space O(k) call stack, k = number of calls
files.output_note: `1 2 3 4 5` (one per line), then a single `5`, then `Sum from 1 to 5 is 15`. The lone 5 appears because `print_five_to_one` was started at 5, so only one call prints. Start it at 1 to see `5 4 3 2 1`.
files.watch_out: The name `print_five_to_one(5)` suggests it prints 5..1, but starting at 5 prints only 5. Call `print_five_to_one(1)`.

check.a: 5, 4, 3 on separate lines: calls go 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 (stop), and printing happens while returning.

files.title: Factorial with recursion
files.what: Computes n! as `n * fact(n-1)`, stopping at 1.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) call stack
files.watch_out: `fact(0)` never hits the base case and recurses until the stack overflows; use `if (n <= 1) return 1;`. `int` overflows from 13! on.

check.q: How many calls does `fact(5)` make in total?
check.a: Five: fact(5), fact(4), fact(3), fact(2), fact(1).

files.title: Fibonacci with plain recursion
files.what: The textbook definition turned into code: `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)`, with `fib(0) = 0`, `fib(1) = 1`.
steps: The same values are recomputed again and again, so the call tree doubles at each level.
files.output_note: Prints `55`, the 10th Fibonacci number. Try 45 and notice how slow it gets.

check.q: Why is this version slow for n = 45?
check.a: It solves the same subproblems many times; the number of calls grows roughly like 1.6^n (over a billion here).

files.title: Fibonacci with memoization (top-down DP)
files.what: Same recursion, but each answer is saved in `dp[n]` the first time, so every n is computed only once.
steps: `memset(dp, -1, sizeof(dp))` marks every state as 'not computed'.
If `dp[n] != -1`, return the saved value at once.
Otherwise compute `fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)`, store it in `dp[n]`, and return it.
files.input_note: A single n (the answer fits in int up to n = 46).
files.output_note: Prints `102334155` (fib(40)) instantly, while the plain recursive version takes noticeably long for n = 40.
files.watch_out: Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: Why is -1 a safe 'empty' marker here?
check.a: Fibonacci values are never negative, so -1 can never be a real stored answer.

files.title: Fibonacci bottom-up (tabulation)
files.what: Builds the table `fibo[0..n]` from the bottom with a loop.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) (can be O(1) with two variables)
files.output_note: Prints `55`, the same answer as the recursive versions.
files.watch_out: For n = 0 the array has size 1 but the code writes `fibo[1]`, which is out of bounds. Handle n = 0 separately or size the array `n + 2`.

check.q: How could you compute fib(n) with O(1) extra memory?
check.a: Keep only the last two values in two variables and update them in the loop.

files.title: LeetCode 70: Climbing Stairs
files.what: To reach step n you arrive from step n-1 or n-2, so ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), with ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2. Solved with memoized recursion.
steps: Base case: for `n < 3` the answer is `n` (1 way for one step, 2 ways for two steps).
files.input_note: A single n. This is LeetCode's Example 2 (expected 3).
files.watch_out: The file only holds the `Solution` class (no includes, no `main`); the page adds a test driver.

check.q: How many ways are there to climb 5 steps?

files.title: Print digits using recursion

problem.name: Codeforces Group - Print Digits using Recursion

files.what: Prints the digits of N left to right, separated by spaces. Recurse on `n/10` first, then print the last digit, so digits come out in the right order.
steps: Base case: a one-digit `n` is printed directly.
Otherwise call `printDigits(n / 10)` to print all digits except the last.
`main` repeats this for T numbers, ending each with a newline.
files.complexity: Time O(number of digits) · Space O(number of digits)
files.output_note: Lines `1 2 1`, `0`, `9 0 2 1 0`. Zero works because it hits the one-digit base case; inner zeros of 90210 are printed normally.

check.q: What would be printed for 123 if the `cout` came before the recursive call?
check.a: The digits in reverse: 3 then 2 then 1.

files.title: Factorial (up to N = 20)
files.what: Same recursive factorial as the lesson, but the judge allows N up to 20.
steps: Read N and print the result.
files.input_note: A single N (1 to 20). 20 is the largest allowed value.
files.output_note: Prints `-2102132736`, a wrong negative number: 20! = 2432902008176640000 does not fit in `int`.
files.watch_out: The function returns `int`, which overflows from 13! on. Change it to `long long factorial(long long n)`; 20! fits in `long long`.

check.q: What is the largest n whose factorial fits in a signed 32-bit int?

files.title: Reach Value (multiply by 10 or 20)
files.what: Works backwards from N: if N is divisible by 10 try N/10, if divisible by 20 try N/20. Reaching exactly 1 means YES.
steps: `canReach(1)` is true; anything below 1 is false.
A `visited` set stops the search from checking the same number twice.
files.complexity: Time O(log N) states per test · Space O(log N)
files.input_note: T, then T values of N. This is the judge's example.
files.output_note: `YES NO YES NO YES` on separate lines, matching the judge. 200 = 1 x 10 x 20, while 25 is not divisible by 10 or 20.

check.q: Why go backwards (divide) instead of forwards (multiply)?
check.a: Dividing only has an option when the number is divisible, so the search stays tiny and ends at 1 or a dead end. Multiplying forward has no natural stopping point except passing N.

files.title: LeetCode 509: Fibonacci Number (bottom-up)
files.what: Bottom-up table: handle n = 0 and n = 1, then fill `dp[2..n]`.
files.input_note: A single n. This is LeetCode's Example 3 (expected 3).
files.watch_out: The file only holds the `Solution` class; it uses `memset` without includes, so the page adds `<bits/stdc++.h>` and a test driver. The `memset` is not even needed because every used cell is written before it is read.

check.q: Why does the fixed-size `dp[31]` work here?
check.a: LeetCode limits n to 30, so indices 0..30 are enough.

files.title: LeetCode 1137: N-th Tribonacci Number
files.what: Like Fibonacci but each term is the sum of the previous **three**. Bottom-up table starting from 0, 1, 1.
steps: Return early for n = 0 (0) and n = 1 or 2 (1).
files.input_note: A single n. This is LeetCode's Example 2 (expected 1389537).
files.watch_out: The file only holds the `Solution` class; the page adds a test driver.

recap: Recursion = base case + a call on a smaller problem.
Code before the call runs on the way down; code after it runs on the way back up.
Repeated subproblems make plain recursion exponential; memoize them with a `dp` array.
Bottom-up loops fill the same table without recursion.
Pick `long long` when values grow fast, and include `<cstring>` when you use `memset`.

check_yourself.q: What are the two ingredients a problem needs for DP to help?
check_yourself.a: Overlapping subproblems (the same smaller question appears many times) and optimal substructure (the answer is built from answers to smaller questions).

check_yourself.q: Top-down or bottom-up: which one can overflow the call stack for n = 10^6?
check_yourself.a: Top-down, because it recurses about n levels deep. Bottom-up uses a loop.

check_yourself.q: How many distinct states does memoized fib(n) compute?

body: Fibonacci numbers are the ones where each is the sum of the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. That rule is almost the definition of recursion, so you can write it down without thinking.

It is correct, and for small `n` it is fast. Ask it for `fib(50)` and the program sits there for minutes. Nothing is broken. It is doing an astonishing amount of repeated work, and seeing exactly where that repetition lives is the point of this module.
Draw the calls for `fib(5)`. It asks for `fib(4)` and `fib(3)`, each of those asks two more, and so on down to 0 and 1.

Look at the picture, not at the code. `fib(3)` appears twice. `fib(2)` appears three times. Each time it is worked out again from nothing, as if the program had never seen it before. That is what **overlapping subproblems** means: the same small question keeps coming back. Count the calls and the damage is plain — the total roughly doubles for every step of `n`, which is about 2^n work and hopeless past 40.
The fix is embarrassingly small: keep a notebook. The first time you work an answer out, write it down; every later time, read it instead of working it out again. That is all **memoisation** is.

The notebook is an array called `dp`, one slot per question, filled with -1 to mean "not answered yet". It is not a list of Fibonacci numbers planned in advance — it is a record of answers already found, indexed by the question that produced them, so `dp[4]` means "the answer to `fib(4)`". Watch it fill while `fib(5)` runs.
intro.trace:
index     0   1   2   3   4   5
start    -1  -1  -1  -1  -1  -1
later     0   1   1  -1  -1  -1
later     0   1   1   2   3  -1
end       0   1   1   2   3   5

the second fib(3) reads dp[3] and returns at once

body: The count collapses. Every value of `n` is computed once, so the work is about `n` steps instead of 2^n. `fib(50)` drops from roughly 40 billion calls to about a hundred and answers instantly.

**What is new.** Recursion you know. Arrays you know. The new thing is giving the recursion a memory, so a question already answered is never re-opened. That combination is dynamic programming, and everything later in the course is a harder version of this one move.

**There are two directions to fill the same table.** Top-down is what you just saw: begin at the big question, recurse downwards, store on the way back up. Bottom-up drops the recursion, begins at the smallest cases and walks forwards with a loop. Same table, same values, opposite order of arrival — and no stack to overflow.

**Two more examples.** Climbing a staircase of `n` steps one or two at a time: the number of ways to reach step `n` is the ways to reach `n-1` plus the ways to reach `n-2`, which is Fibonacci wearing a hat. Tribonacci is the same again with three terms instead of two. In the "reach value" problem the remembered thing is a set of values already tried, so no value is explored twice — a different notebook, the same idea.

**When it does not help.** Memoisation only pays if the same question genuinely comes back; if every call is a fresh question, the notebook fills and is never read. And these numbers grow fast, so reach for `long long`: 13! already overflows an `int`.
The programs below walk the same road slowly — plain recursion, the call tree, memoisation, the bottom-up loop, then five practice problems.
